title: Why Did Easter Island's Civilization Collapse?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine the long-told story of the Rapa Nui (Easter Island) civilization's collapse, popularized by Jared Diamond's 2005 book Collapse, which blamed deforestation, famine, civil war and a birdman cult. They outline the island's settlement by Hotu Matua's family from Polynesia, the moai statues and how they may have been moved, and Admiral Jacob Roggeveen's 1722 arrival. They then cover newer archaeological interpretations (Hunt, Lipo, Mulrooney) that question population collapse, argue rats caused the loss of trees, describe the "matā" spearheads as farm tools, and frame the story as one of adaptation. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about the Thousand Girls Initiative in Guatemala from the Cooperative for Education (CoEd) and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and Rapa Nui name
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, then discuss the name Rapa Nui, Kevin Reynolds films, and their frustration with a HowStuffWorks article that treats the collapse story as settled fact.

segments.title: Jared Diamond and the collapse narrative
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Jared Diamond's 2005 book Collapse popularized the story of Easter Island's self-inflicted collapse, and that oral traditions recorded in the 1880s are considered unreliable.

segments.title: Easter Island naming and Roggeveen
segments.summary: The island's Spanish name Isla de Pascua and English name Easter Island come from Dutch admiral Jacob Roggeveen's arrival on Easter Sunday 1722; he was looking for an island described by pirate Edward Davis.

segments.title: The moai and early island settlement
segments.summary: Introduction to the moai statues, the Rapa Nui people, and Hotu Matua, the first chief who allegedly arrived by canoe from Polynesia with his family, bringing plants such as taro.

segments.title: Island environment, settlement and social structure
segments.summary: Describes the island's original palm forests, scarce marine food, and early settlement around a thousand years ago; the clan-based society, chiefs and mana, and the spiritual role of ancestors and moai.

segments.title: Carving and transporting the moai
segments.summary: Moai were carved from volcanic tuff at Rano Raraku; the largest, El Gigante, is about 70 feet and unfinished. Theories of how they were moved include log sledges (Joe Van Tilburg test), and walking them with ropes (Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt test).

segments.title: Roggeveen's arrival, population decline and birdman cult
segments.summary: Roggeveen's arrival and the violence he used; the discrepancy between the number of abandoned moai and the population he estimated; the traditional collapse narrative of deforestation, erosion, starvation, civil war, and the birdman cult with its egg contest.

segments.title: Chilean annexation and the new interpretation
segments.summary: European contact, Spanish and Chilean annexation, and population dropping to about 110 by the late 1800s. Newer research by Mulrooney, Hunt and Lipo questions the population collapse, proposes rats as the cause of tree loss, reinterprets the matā as farm tools, and describes soil improvement and rat eating as adaptation.

segments.title: Krulwich commentary and podcast chatter
segments.summary: Robert Krulwich's reading of the Rapa Nui story as a lesson about adapting to climate change, followed by banter about Radiolab and podcaster friends.

segments.title: Listener mail: Thousand Girls Initiative in Guatemala
segments.summary: A listener from CoEd relays news of the Thousand Girls Initiative, which lets sponsors pay $35 or $70 a month to keep a Guatemalan girl in school, with a link to thousandgirlsinitiative.org. The hosts also invite listeners to get in touch and sign off.
